subject: english-language-and-literature
title: English Language and Literature MYP 5 eAssessment Structure Mock A (7 tasks, 80 marks)

questions.content:
[[Q 1.1 | A 2]]
Task 1: Analysing
Questions 1.1 to 1.4 focus on the key concept of communication. Question 1.5 focuses on the key concept of connections. The criteria assessed are A (Analysing) and B (Organizing). Suggested time for Questions 1.1 to 1.4: 15 minutes. Suggested time for Question 1.5: 35 minutes.

Text A: 'The Spice Tin' (an extract from a short story, written for this paper)
This extract describes Rania, a girl who has recently arrived in England, on the evening a parcel from her mother reaches her.

The tin arrived in the second week of November, wrapped in a jumper that smelled of someone else's house. Rania carried it up the stairs of the flat as if it might spill, though the lid was sealed with tape, and set it on the windowsill beside the radiator, where the cold glass of an English evening pressed against it.

On the lid her mother had written in Arabic, in the looping hand that had once signed every one of Rania's school reports: for the soup that cures things. Rania did not open it. She knew what she would find: cumin, coriander, the dark crumbs of dried lime, all ground by her grandmother's wrists in a kitchen in a city that no airline flew to any more.

Downstairs, the neighbours' television laughed at something. Somebody was frying onions, but they were the wrong onions. The smell was too thin, too polite.

At school she had been Rania for two months, which is to say she had been Ray-nee-a, then Rainy, then, whenever Mr Whitfield took the register, a brief and hopeful silence while he searched the page for how she was supposed to sound. She had stopped correcting him. Correcting took energy she needed for the other work: the daily labour of arranging her face into a person who was fine.

On the phone her mother said, "You are eating? You are speaking English all day?" and Rania said yes to both, because yes was the shortest road to the end of the call.

Now she lifted the tin and held it against her chest. It weighed almost nothing. It weighed everything. When she finally prised off the tape and the lid, the smell rose like a hand laid on the back of her neck, and for a moment the radiator, the rain, the wrong onions, all of it went quiet.

She said her own name aloud, slowly, the way her grandmother used to, with the rolled r that English had no room for. Rania. Rania. It sounded like a door she had not realised was still unlocked.

Text B: webpage for 'Suitcase Stories', a community exhibition (written for this paper; in the live exam this would be a screen image)

[Layout: A wide banner photograph fills the top of the page. An open brown leather suitcase rests on a bare wooden floor. It holds no clothes. Instead it is crammed with small objects: a dented kettle, a school photograph, a paper bag of seeds, a football scarf and a child's red shoe. The light falls softly from the left. Across a deep teal band beneath the photograph, in large white capitals, are the words:]

WHAT WOULD YOU CARRY?

[Subheading in white italics:] Twenty-six people. Twenty-six suitcases. One city that is still learning to call itself home.

[The page divides into two columns below a thin gold line.]

[Left column, heading in teal capitals:] THE EXHIBITION
Every object here has crossed a border. Some arrived in a pocket, some in the back of a lorry, some only in the memory of a person who had to leave the real thing behind. For six weeks they sit under glass at Eastfield Library, beside the words of the people who carried them. Come and listen.

[A small photograph sits beneath this text: an elderly man holding a chipped enamel cup in both hands and looking just past the camera. Caption in grey italics:] Tomasz, 74, carried this cup from Gdansk in 1981. "It is worth nothing. That is why it is worth everything."

[Right column, heading in teal capitals:] JOIN IN
- Bring one object and tell us its story (open table, every Saturday, 2 p.m.)
- Record a message in your first language for our listening wall
- Help us translate the labels into twenty languages

[A bright yellow button, centred below both columns, reads:] ADD YOUR STORY

[A pull quote in large serif type is set between two thin lines across the full width of the page:] "Home is not only where you come from. It is what you refuse to leave behind."

[Footer in small grey type:] Free entry. Step-free access. 14 March to 30 April. A project of Eastfield Library and the Eastfield Welcome Network.

Q 1.1 Comment on the use of the senses in the first two paragraphs of Text A. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 2 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a sense or sensory detail with a reference to the text but does not explain its effect, e.g. 'a jumper that smelled of someone else's house' appeals to smell. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): comments on the use of the senses with an example and some explanation, e.g. smell ('someone else's house'), touch ('the cold glass of an English evening pressed against it') and sight ('the looping hand') build a sense of Rania's loneliness in an unfamiliar place and make the parcel feel precious as a link with her mother. [1] Accept any valid sense and effect (hearing is not yet used in these paragraphs). Award 0 for no or incorrect reference to the text.

questions.content:
[[Q 1.2 | A 3]]
Refer to Text A (printed in Question 1.1). Explain the effect of the lines: 'Somebody was frying onions, but they were the wrong onions. The smell was too thin, too polite.' (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 3 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies an effect without developing it, e.g. the lines show that Rania misses her home. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes an effect with some example or explanation, e.g. the repeated 'wrong onions' shows that even ordinary smells are foreign to her, so she feels she does not belong. [1] Level 3 (3 marks): explains the effect consistently with well-chosen quotation, e.g. the personification of the smell as 'too polite' suggests the new country is courteous but distant and cold, contrasted with the warmth of the spices; the short, flat sentence rhythm after the longer sentence echoes her sense of disappointment and isolation. [1] Accept any valid reading supported by the text.

questions.content:
[[Q 1.3 | A 2]]
Refer to Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Describe the purpose of the question 'WHAT WOULD YOU CARRY?' in the banner. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 2 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a purpose without explanation, e.g. it makes the reader think. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes the purpose with an example or explanation, e.g. the direct question addresses the reader personally and invites them to imagine being forced to leave home, so that they feel empathy before reading about the exhibition; the large capitals on teal make it the first thing the eye sees and catch attention. [1] Accept: to engage and involve the audience; to introduce the theme of what matters most.

questions.content:
[[Q 1.4 | A 3]]
Refer to Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Analyse the effect of a technique used in Text B. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 3 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a technique and an effect with no development, e.g. there is a photograph of a suitcase. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes the effect of one technique with some justification, e.g. the suitcase holds everyday objects such as a kettle and a child's shoe, which makes the migrants' lives seem familiar and human to the reader. [1] Level 3 (3 marks): analyses the effect consistently with a precise example, e.g. the caption quotation 'It is worth nothing. That is why it is worth everything.' uses paradox and a personal voice to show that value is emotional, not financial, and the contrast with the gentle grey caption text makes the old man's words stand out; or the imperative button 'ADD YOUR STORY' turns the audience from observers into participants. [1] Accept any valid technique: layout, colour, imagery, list structure, repetition of 'Twenty-six', pull quote, direct address.

questions.content:
[[Q 1.5 | A 10 | B 10]]
Refer to Text A and Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Compare and contrast how the concept of identity is explored in the two texts. (Approximately 350 words) (20 marks)

Criterion A (Analysing) is worth 10 marks and Criterion B (Organizing) is worth 10 marks.
questions.mark_scheme: Total 20 marks: Criterion A (10) and Criterion B (10). Criterion A Analysing (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): identifies some content, language, structure or technique with few or no examples; little sense of how the texts relate. 3-4 (adequate): describes some features of the texts with some examples; a degree of understanding of how features create meaning; some awareness of similarity or difference. 5-6 (considerable): explains the effect of a range of features with relevant examples from both texts; clear understanding of how meaning is created; sound awareness of similarities and differences. 7-8 (substantial): analyses the effect of content, language, structure and technique in both texts with well-chosen evidence; thoughtful understanding of the writers' and creators' choices and of the relationship between the texts. 9-10 (excellent): perceptive, sustained analysis of both texts with precise, well-integrated evidence; insightful evaluation of how and why meaning is shaped, and a discerning view of the relationship between the texts. Indicative content for A (not exhaustive; credit any valid, evidenced point). Text A: identity under pressure; the mispronounced name (Ray-nee-a, Rainy) and the 'person who was fine' show a self that is diminished and masked; the tin, the smell and the grandmother's pronunciation carry identity across distance; third-person limited narration and the final door metaphor create a private, quiet moment of reclaiming the self; imagery of senses and sentence rhythm. Text B: identity as shared, collective and public; objects and stories are displayed so that identity is recorded, respected and celebrated; the use of numbers ('Twenty-six'), the direct address of the question, the caption voice of Tomasz, the pull quote and the invitation to participate; the multimodal layout moves the audience from empathy to action. Similarities: both use ordinary objects (tin, cup, suitcase) as symbols of belonging; both link identity to memory, language and home; both ask the audience to value what has been left behind. Differences: private, painful and unresolved in Text A versus public, hopeful and communal in Text B; fiction showing one voice versus an informative and persuasive text showing many; narrative interiority versus direct address. Award up to [10] for Criterion A. Criterion B Organizing (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): little structure; the texts are mostly treated separately or in a list; ideas are hard to follow; little or no concluding thought. 3-4 (adequate): some structure with an opening and a close; both texts are discussed with a few links; some paragraphing and a degree of coherence. 5-6 (considerable): a clear structure; comparison and contrast appear in most paragraphs; ideas are generally logical and linked; an appropriate conclusion. 7-8 (substantial): an effective, purposeful structure; comparison and contrast are woven through the response; transitions are controlled and ideas build; a developed conclusion. 9-10 (excellent): a sophisticated, fully controlled structure that shapes the argument; comparison and contrast are integrated throughout; seamless linking; a conclusion that synthesizes the argument. Look for a comparative structure (for example by idea or by technique), topic sentences that name both texts, comparative connectives (whereas, similarly, in contrast) and a conclusion. Award up to [10] for Criterion B.

questions.content:
[[Q 2 | C 10 | D 10]]
Task 2: Producing literary text
This task focuses on the key concept of creativity. The criteria assessed are C (Producing text) and D (Using language). Suggested time: 35 minutes.

Image 1 (described in words): a single battered suitcase stands alone on a deserted railway platform at dusk. The last carriage of a train, its windows lit orange, is pulling away into the distance. A yellow lamp flickers overhead and rain gleams on the platform.
Image 2 (described in words): the inside of a kitchen window, steamed up on a winter morning. Someone has drawn a small heart in the condensation and, beside it, pressed a child's handprint, through which the street outside is blurred into grey and gold.

Using one of the images, write the opening of a story about a character who must leave something behind, or who returns to something they have left behind. You may consider purpose, characterisation, setting, mood and point of view. State which image you are using before you start. (Approximately 350 words) (20 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Total 20 marks: Criterion C (10) and Criterion D (10). Criterion C Producing text (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): limited creative choices; little imagination or insight; little detail; the image or prompt is hardly used. 3-4 (adequate): some creative choices; some imagination and insight; some relevant detail; the image and prompt are used in a basic way. 5-6 (considerable): thoughtful creative choices of content, character, setting and point of view; considerable imagination and insight; sufficient relevant detail. 7-8 (substantial): purposeful, imaginative choices; a developed voice and perspective; substantial insight; well-chosen detail that supports a clear purpose. 9-10 (excellent): highly original, perceptive choices; an assured, distinctive voice and perspective; extensive, precise detail and a controlled narrative or poetic shape that fully serves the prompt. A response that uses neither image and does not address the prompt scores 0 for Criterion C. Indicative content: the named image is clearly used as a starting point; a character with a believable reason to leave or return; a controlled setting and mood (for example transience, nostalgia, uncertainty); sensory detail; a deliberate point of view; an opening that creates curiosity. Credit narrative, descriptive or poetic forms if they work as an opening. Award up to [10] for Criterion C. Criterion D Using language (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): limited range of vocabulary and structures; errors are frequent and often hinder communication; register is rarely appropriate. 3-4 (adequate): adequate range; a degree of accuracy; errors sometimes hinder communication; register is sometimes appropriate. 5-6 (considerable): a varied range of vocabulary, sentence structures and devices; considerable accuracy; errors do not hinder communication; register and style are generally appropriate. 7-8 (substantial): an effective range used with control; high accuracy with occasional slips; register and style are consistently appropriate and purposeful. 9-10 (excellent): a sophisticated, flexible range used with precision and flair; highly accurate with only minor errors; register and style are skilfully sustained throughout. Look for varied sentence length, precise verbs and imagery, effective control of tense, and accurate punctuation of dialogue where used. Award up to [10] for Criterion D.

questions.content:
[[Q 3 | B 10 | C 10 | D 10]]
Task 3: Producing non-literary text
This task focuses on the key concept of perspective. You will create a piece of non-literary writing in relation to the global context orientation in space and time: migration and the movement of people. The criteria assessed are B (Organizing), C (Producing text) and D (Using language). Suggested time: 50 minutes.

Write a feature article for your school magazine under the title 'Between Two Places' about what it means to belong to more than one place or culture, and what a welcoming school community can do to help newcomers feel they belong. Use a clear structure and the conventions of a feature article, such as a headline, an engaging opening, a balance of personal voice and evidence, and a closing thought. (Approximately 350 words) (30 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Total 30 marks: Criterion B (10), Criterion C (10) and Criterion D (10). Criterion B Organizing (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): little organisation; few or no text-type conventions; ideas not sequenced; paragraphing absent or random. 3-4 (adequate): some organisation; some conventions of the text type are used; a basic opening and ending; paragraphing is mostly logical. 5-6 (considerable): a clear structure; most conventions of the text type are used appropriately; ideas are generally sequenced and linked. 7-8 (substantial): an effective structure; conventions of the text type used purposefully; clear progression with controlled links and an effective opening and close. 9-10 (excellent): a skilfully crafted structure; conventions of the text type exploited for effect; seamless progression, with every paragraph contributing to the purpose and audience. Indicative content: headline and possible standfirst; a hook (an anecdote, a striking image or a question); developed paragraphs on belonging and identity; examples drawn from school life, language, food, friendship or traditions; a quotation or interview, real or imagined; a balanced call to action; a closing line that links back to the opening. Award up to [10] for Criterion B. Criterion C Producing text (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): little insight into the global context or topic; little relevant detail; limited sense of audience and purpose. 3-4 (adequate): some insight into the global context; some relevant detail and examples; some awareness of audience and purpose. 5-6 (considerable): considerable insight into the global context and the topic; sufficient relevant detail and examples; a clear perspective and a good sense of audience and purpose. 7-8 (substantial): substantial, well-developed insight; well-chosen examples that support the argument; an assured perspective and a controlled appeal to the audience. 9-10 (excellent): perceptive, original insight into the global context; extensive, precise detail and examples; a distinctive, convincing perspective that fully serves the audience and purpose. Indicative content: insight into migration as both loss and gain; the experience of newcomers and of those who welcome them; specific, plausible suggestions such as buddy systems, language clubs, shared meals and a curriculum that reflects many histories; awareness that identity can be plural. Award up to [10] for Criterion C. Criterion D Using language (10 marks). 0: no work that meets a descriptor. 1-2 (limited): limited range of vocabulary and structures; errors are frequent and often hinder communication; register is rarely appropriate. 3-4 (adequate): adequate range; a degree of accuracy; errors sometimes hinder communication; register is sometimes appropriate. 5-6 (considerable): a varied range of vocabulary, sentence structures and devices; considerable accuracy; errors do not hinder communication; register and style are generally appropriate. 7-8 (substantial): an effective range used with control; high accuracy with occasional slips; register and style are consistently appropriate and purposeful. 9-10 (excellent): a sophisticated, flexible range used with precision and flair; highly accurate with only minor errors; register and style are skilfully sustained throughout. Look for an engaging journalistic register that is semi-formal, rhetorical devices used purposefully (rule of three, anecdote, inclusive pronouns, rhetorical question), and accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. Award up to [10] for Criterion D.
